newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Grim New Year for Manila death row inmates.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Grim New Year for Manila death row inmates.

text.p: A hilltop construction site to the south of Manila is humming with activity but gives some in the vicinity a sense of grim foreboding.
Workers will complete by the end of January, on the hill in the Muntinlupa national penitentiary, the Philippines' only execution chamber.
The air-conditioned single-storey structure will have three telephone hotlines to the presidential palace, will be equipped with closed circuit television and will be under round-the-clock guard.
There have been no executions in the country since 1976 but there are more than 250 people on death row, and all have been transferred to Muntinlupa.

Retired police general Vic Vinarao, the prison chief, says the building will be equipped to carry out executions by lethal injection, which he said was more humane than the electric chair, the gas chamber or hanging.

Vinarao told a Reuters reporter permitted to visit the prison: "In lethal injection, what the death convict will feel is only the prick of the needle," Death would follow in one to three minutes, he added.
DEATH PENALTY RESTORED

The Philippines abolished capital punishment in 1987 and commuted the sentences of those on death row. But it restored the death penalty in 1994 for murder, armed robbery, drug trafficking, rape and kidnapping for ransom.
Since then, 282 people have been sentenced to death. These include a tour guide convicted of raping a British actress, and a Japanese man and two Taiwanese who were all convicted of drug trafficking.
Separated from the rest of the 10,500 prisoners at the sprawling penitentiary, those on death row are now kept in two whitewashed buildings called Dormitories 1C-2 and 1-D.
The Supreme Court, which reviews death sentences, has so far upheld only one, that of house painter Leo Echegaray, 38, who was convicted in 1994 of raping his 10-year-old daughter.
Under Philippine law, executions must be carried out between one year and 18 months after the sentence has been confirmed by the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court confirmed Echegary's sentence in June 1996. He could therefore become the first to be executed at the new building, between June and the end of 1997, unless he is granted a presidential reprieve.
Prison guards permitted Echegary to be interviewed.
"I don't want to die yet," he said, bursting into tears and refusing to speak further.

Tour guide Silvino Salarza, convicted in 1994 for the rape of a British actress in a Palawan island beach house, said the only reason he was on death row was because he could not afford a good lawyer.
"When they hang a rich man, that's the time I will believe in justice," Salarza said.
EXECUTION PROCEDURE
Vinarao said condemned convicts will be taken to the execution chamber one day before the sentence is to be carried out. They will spend their last night in a bedroom with padded walls.
On the day itself, the condemned person will be taken by four guards to the main chamber, and strapped to a bed with arm-rests.

Three telephone links in the chamber are hotlines to the presidential palace, in case of a last-minute reprieve. If there is no call by the set execution time, three quick injections will be administered by specially-trained paramedical staff.
The first injection will clear the vein, the second will induce sleep and the third will stop the heart.
Government officials, relatives of the convict and media will be allowed to watch through one-way glass set up in two rooms next to the chamber.

Of 102 people executed in the Philippines this century, a total of 84 -- all Filipinos -- died in the electric chair. Seventeen Japanese soldiers were hanged after World War Two and a Chinese narcotics dealer was shot by firing squad under martial law in 1972.

Officials say it the lethal injection is less costly than a gas chamber or electric chair. A gas chamber would cost $230,000 to build, while $100,000 would be needed to buy a new electric chair. The injection chamber will cost about $38,000 to build and the injection itself just $50.
Vinarao said the chamber, when in operation, will have a deterrent effect on criminals. "Then people will realise that the government means business," he said.
